section-bus.snapshot:
- main:
  - navigation "Breadcrumb":
    - link "Home":
      - /url: /
    - text: Bus
  - link "Back to the home page":
    - /url: /
  - heading "Bus" [level=1]
  - paragraph: How Taipei's joint-operation bus network is numbered, coloured and paid for.
  - heading "Network All network →" [level=2]:
    - text: Network
    - link "All network →":
      - /url: /bus/network/
  - paragraph: The joint-operation system — one brand, one fare structure, many private companies — and the route numbering that encodes more than it appears to.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - link "The joint-operation network Around 280 routes, fourteen private companies and one brand. Four city regulations set out how the money actually moves — and the central revenue pool everyone repeats is in none of them.":
        - /url: /bus/network/joint-operation/
  - paragraph:
    - text: "Taipei's city buses run as 聯營公車 — a joint operation: private companies operating under one fare structure, one numbering scheme and one brand, so that to a passenger it looks like a single network when it is not. That structural fact — how many companies, how many routes, and the four city regulations that actually set out how the money moves — is explained in full on"
    - link "the joint-operation network":
      - /url: /bus/network/joint-operation/
    - text: .
  - heading "What comes next" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - strong: The network itself, before anything else.
    - text: Taipei's city buses run as 聯營公車 — a joint operation. Private companies operate under one fare structure, one numbering scheme and one brand, so that to a passenger it looks like a single network when it is not. That structural fact is the most valuable thing this section can explain, almost no English source states it, and it is why
    - link "Network":
      - /url: /bus/network/
    - text: sits above the operator and route pages rather than below them.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Operators.
    - text: More than a dozen companies work the network under contract, each with its own fleet, liveries and garages. The relationships between them — including who owns whom — are poorly documented in English, which makes this the part most likely to be worth reading rather than merely present.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Routes.
    - text: The trunk corridors to begin with — the numbered services and the bus lanes along Zhongxiao, Renai, Xinyi and Nanjing — rather than attempting the lot. Taipei City and New Taipei between them run several hundred routes, and a few hundred stub pages would be worth less than twenty written ones. The route
    - emphasis: numbering system
    - text: itself needs an explainer before any route page makes sense.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Vehicles and garages.
    - text: Fleet lists exist through enthusiast sources and operator publications; they churn constantly, which is why
    - link "Models":
      - /url: /bus/models/
    - text: and
    - link "Garages":
      - /url: /bus/garages/
    - text: wait for a data pipeline rather than a transcription.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Fares and payment.
    - text: Section-based fares, the EasyCard transfer discount between bus and metro, and where the section boundaries actually fall — which is the thing visitors get wrong most often.
  - paragraph: "Operators and routes come after the network explainer rather than alongside it, for a reason specific to buses: metro station data comes from MOTC's open data platform — authoritative, stable, slow to change. Bus route data is published per-operator and per-municipality, changes far more often, and the English-language versions of it go out of date quickly. Covering it honestly needs a data pipeline rather than a transcription, so operator and route pages wait on that rather than on effort."
  - paragraph:
    - text: See
    - link "about":
      - /url: /about/
    - text: for how this site sources material.

      - text: There is no cab. Stand at the front of the leading car and the guideway comes straight at you — through the hills above

      - text: The Wenhu Line was

    - heading "The alignment was redrawn by protest before a metre of it was built" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The route that opened in 1996 is not the route that was approved
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: . A 13 km scheme from
      - link "Taipei Zoo":
        - /url: /rail/stations/br01/
      - text: to
      - link "Liuzhangli":
        - /url: /rail/stations/br07/
      - text: had already been settled when
      - strong: residents in Muzha objected, and on 4 May the northern section was redirected onto Fuxing South and North Roads
      - text: — where it runs today
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "That is the earliest instance of a pattern this site records twice more: the"
      - link "Songshan–Xindian Line":
        - /url: /rail/lines/songshan-xindian-line/
      - text: redesigned from part-elevated to fully underground in 1987 on street-width and visual-impact grounds, and the Neihu extension held up for years over the same argument.
      - strong: The objection came first, before the line existed, and it worked.
      - text: What exactly was moved, and which proposed stations went with it, is not established here and is worth a proper look.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The original section was bought in 1988 as a turnkey system from France's Matra
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: . What followed —
      - strong: two fires during testing in 1993
      - text: ", on 5 May and 24 September, the second recorded as exactly that, 第二次火燒車事件, a second vehicle-fire incident"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: ; an opening four and a quarter years late; the builder's withdrawal from maintaining its own system; and a lawsuit that ran until the Supreme Court ordered the city to pay roughly NT$1.64 billion in 2005
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: "— is told in full on its own page:"
      - strong:
        - link "The Matra dispute":
          - /url: /rail/history/matra-dispute/
      - text: . The short version is that Taipei learned, expensively, how not to buy a railway, and bought the second half differently.
    - paragraph:
      - text: When the Neihu extension opened on 4 July 2009, the two sections began running as one through line under the extension's new CITYFLO 650 signalling
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: . The original VAL256 fleet was withdrawn that same day for conversion to the new system and did not carry passengers again until 26 December 2010
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: — eighteen months in which the 1996 railway ran entirely on the 2009 trains. See
      - link "VAL256":
        - /url: /rail/rolling-stock/val256/
      - text: .
    - heading "Route" [level=2]
    - paragraph: Elevated for almost its entire length. From BR01 the line climbs north through Wenshan District, crosses central Taipei on an east–west alignment, then turns north-east across the Keelung River into Neihu.
    - paragraph:
      - strong:
        - text: "Two of the twenty-four stations are underground: BR13"
        - link "Songshan Airport":
          - /url: /rail/stations/br13/
        - text: and BR14
        - link "Dazhi":
          - /url: /rail/stations/br14/
      - text: ", and both are now settled by DORTS itself rather than inferred."
    - paragraph:
      - text: The builder's project record gives the Neihu section as 14.8 km with 「地下段3.9公里，2座地下站」 — 3.9 km underground, two underground stations
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: "— which narrows the pair to BR13 – BR24 without naming them. Its station architecture page then names one of the two and counts the rest: 「除大直站為地下車站外，其餘共有十座高架車站」, apart from Dazhi being underground, the remaining ten are elevated"
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: . Ten elevated plus Dazhi is eleven of the section's twelve stations, and the project record says there are exactly two underground
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: . The twelfth station is Songshan Airport, so Songshan Airport is the second. Two primary documents that never mention each other, and the identification falls out of the arithmetic between them. zh.wikipedia names the same pair outright
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: ; it is no longer what the claim rests on.
    - paragraph: The platform depths are still not established here and are not asserted.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Every platform on the line has full-height platform screen doors: Faiveley equipment from BR01 to BR12 , ST Electronics from BR13 to BR24"
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: .
    - heading "How many ways out" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS's station table counts the street exits at every station, and the distribution is lopsided in a way that says something about how the line was built
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Eight of the twenty-four stations have exactly one exit
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: ", and seven of those eight are consecutive: BR02 Muzha through BR08 Technology Building, an unbroken run from Wenshan into"
      - link "Daan":
        - /url: /rail/stations/r05/
      - text: where every station has one way in and one way out. BR12
      - link "Zhongshan Junior High School":
        - /url: /rail/stations/br12/
      - text: is the eighth
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Twenty of the twenty-four have three exits or fewer. The whole line has sixty-three between its twenty-four stations, and a quarter of those are at two stations: BR11"
      - link "Nanjing Fuxing":
        - /url: /rail/stations/g16/
      - text: and BR24
      - link "Nangang":
        - /url: /rail/stations/bl22/
      - text: Exhibition Center have eight each. BR09 Daan has six, BR10
      - link "Zhongxiao Fuxing":
        - /url: /rail/stations/bl15/
      - text: five. All four are interchanges
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: That is not a trivia column. A single-exit station is one lift, one stair, one escalator bank and one crowd; when it closes, the station closes. It is a predictable consequence of building a medium-capacity railway on a single row of columns down the middle of an existing road — the same constraint DORTS gives for why these stations carry no decoration, which is that a single-column support system limits what you can hang on it
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: . The exits are the same economy, at street level.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Every station page carries its own count, from the same table
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - strong:
        - text: BR06
        - link "Linguang":
          - /url: /rail/stations/br06/
        - text: is the exception that proves the constraint was real.
      - text: It has two exits and it is the first station on the
      - link "Taipei Metro":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
      - text: that opened with both of them already built
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: — everywhere else, a second exit was something added later or not at all. The same station has
      - strong: two ticket machines, the fewest anywhere on the network
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: .
    - heading "Operations" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Trains run without on-board drivers under automatic train control, at GoA4 — unattended train operation, the highest grade
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: Weekday headways are about 2–4 minutes at peak, 4–10 off-peak, and about 12 minutes after 23:00; weekends and holidays run the off-peak pattern all day
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: .
      - strong: End to end takes about 45 minutes
      - text: ", BR01 to BR24 or the reverse"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: . zh.wikipedia adds that the headway can be compressed to 80 seconds
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: ; that is a signalling capability rather than a timetable, and no primary source for it was found.

      - text: Four figures circulate, and they are not in conflict — they measure four different things.
      - strong: This site publishes 25.17 km, the operating length
      - text: ", and says what each of the others counts."

    - paragraph:
      - text: "The last row is the one this site got wrong: it printed the untrimmed figure as the route length for four builds, because measuring everything MOTC draws counts depot lead and tail track that no passenger travels on"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . Trimmed to the termini, the same geometry lands within 130 m of the operator's own figure
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: — and that agreement is the check working, which is why both are still printed side by side on the
      - link "network page":
        - /url: /rail/network/
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The 25.7 km that appears as 路線長度 on zh.wikipedia
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: is the
      - strong: sum of the two published section lengths
      - text: ": DORTS records 木柵線 約10.9公里 and 內湖線 約14.8公里, and 10.9 + 14.8 = 25.7 exactly"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: . Those are project lengths — the extent of what was built, including non-revenue track at each end — which is why the total exceeds the 25.17 km of railway that carries passengers
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - heading "Rolling stock" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "Two fleets share the line, both running as four cars made up of two coupled pairs:"
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - link "VAL256":
          - /url: /rail/rolling-stock/val256/
        - text: — 51 pairs, the original Muzha Line fleet
        - superscript:
          - link "[11]":
            - /url: "#ref-11"
      - listitem:
        - link "Innovia APM 256 (C370)":
          - /url: /rail/rolling-stock/innovia-apm-256-c370/
        - text: — 101 pairs, delivered for the Neihu extension
        - superscript:
          - link "[12]":
            - /url: "#ref-12"
    - heading "The fleet totals do not divide, and this site cannot say why" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: A four-car train on this line is two coupled pairs. DORTS's procurement record gives
      - strong: 51 pairs of VAL256 and 101 pairs of Innovia
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: . The renewal reporting counts
      - strong: 25 Matra trains and 51 Bombardier trains
      - text: ", 76 in total"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: Those do not reconcile
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: . 25 four-car trains need 50 pairs, not 51; 51 trains need 102 pairs, not 101. The totals agree — 152 pairs, 304 cars, 76 trains
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: — but
      - strong: neither fleet on its own divides into whole trains.
    - paragraph: "Three readings, and nothing found settles between them:"
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - strong: A spare pair in each fleet.
        - text: 25 Matra trains plus one pair out of service, 50 Bombardier trains plus one — which makes the "76 trains" figure a count of the two fleets' nominal sizes rather than of trains in traffic.
      - listitem:
        - strong: Formations are not fixed.
        - text: zh.wikipedia describes the VAL256 as 「非固定編組」, running as four consecutively-numbered cars rather than as a permanent set
        - superscript:
          - link "[5]":
            - /url: "#ref-5"
        - text: . If pairs are re-formed in maintenance, the two counts are simply two different things measured on two different days
        - superscript:
          - link "[5]":
            - /url: "#ref-5"
        - text: ", and there is no discrepancy to explain."
      - listitem:
        - strong: One train is mixed.
        - text: Moving a pair across the boundary makes both counts work — and would mean exactly one train on this line runs one fleet's pair coupled to the other's.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: The third would make this page wrong
      - text: ", because it describes the fleets as separate. It is also the only one of the three that requires something no source found here reports"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: . It is recorded here because leaving it out would be picking an answer quietly.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "They are not the same vehicle and not the same design lineage — the second was built by a competitor to fit the first's guideway, which is the Matra story's last chapter — but the interface they share is exact: the same running-surface spacing, the same side guide bars, the same 750 V taken off them"
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: . TRTC has announced a programme to replace all 76 trains by 2041 — see the research notes, and treat the figures as provisional.
    - heading "Depots" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - link "Muzha Depot":
        - /url: /rail/depots/muzha-depot/
      - text: sits at the southern end beside BR01 and opened with the line in 1996
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: .
      - link "Neihu Depot":
        - /url: /rail/depots/neihu-depot/
      - text: was built for the extension and came into use in 2009
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: . Despite its name it is in Nangang District, and it joins the running line at
      - strong: BR24
      - text: ", at the far end of the line"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: .
    - heading "Sources" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Station names, codes, running order, coordinates and the end-to-end journey time come from
      - strong: Taiwan MOTC's TDX platform
      - text: ", operator TRTC — government open data, retrieved 5 August 2026. The strip map is generated from it directly. Everything else is cited inline and listed below."
    - paragraph: TDX does not publish station structure, headways, or anything about rolling stock and depots; those come from TRTC's and DORTS's own publications where they exist, and are marked secondary where they do not.
    - heading "Corrections" [level=2]
    - paragraph: This page's errors are corrected in place and recorded here, most recent first.
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - strong: The strip map drew Neihu Depot at the wrong end of the line for four builds.
        - text: This page previously said the depot joined the running line near BR19 Neihu — an unsourced inference from the shared name. It actually connects at BR24 , in Nangang District
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":
            - /url: "#ref-2"
        - text: ", and the map marker moved with the fact."
        - code: npm run facts
        - text: now cross-checks the marker against the depot page's own stated junction.
      - listitem:
        - strong: Two engineering superlatives were removed rather than corrected.
        - text: This page used to say the gradients through Wenshan were steeper than conventional heavy metro could manage, and that the elevated curves would be
        - emphasis: impossible
        - text: on a steel-wheel alignment. Both are probably true and neither was sourced, and "impossible" was doing a great deal of unattributed work. They can return when DORTS's design criteria are found.
      - listitem:
        - strong: The 25.7 km figure was described as unaccounted for.
        - text: An earlier version of this page could not say where the widely-circulated 25.7 km came from. It is simply the sum of DORTS's two project lengths, as the length section above now shows.

      - text: The line runs on viaduct for all but 3.9 km of its length, dives under Songshan Airport and the Keelung River, and comes back up beside the south portal of the Ziqiang road tunnel at Dazhi.
      - strong: 3.9 km of the line runs underground.
      - text: "2.58 km of that is between the two underground stations, which is fixed by the operator’s own chainage. The remaining 1.32 km is ramp at the two portals, and no source divides it between them — so it is drawn as unplaced rather than split. The 3.9 km is DORTS's own figure for the Neihu section, and it is the line's only underground running: the builder records the Muzha section as 全線以高架方式興建, built entirely on viaduct. zh.wikipedia's route description reads 穿越福州山隧道後, which implies a tunnel between BR05 and BR06 where DORTS instead has the line passing the north side of the Xinhai road tunnel. A viaduct does not run through a hill, so the drawing follows the builder — but the two accounts of that half-kilometre have not been reconciled. Distance is to scale. Height is not: no source gives a rail level, and an axis invented to look like a measurement would be worse than none."

  - article:
    - heading "Sanying Line" [level=1]
    - paragraph: New Taipei's newest railway — a driverless elevated line to Sanxia and Yingge, open five weeks and still free to ride, written up here while every English source is still a machine translation.
    - region "Quick facts":
      - text: LB Sanying Line 三鶯線
      - term: Operator
      - definition:
        - link "New Taipei Metro Corporation":
          - /url: /rail/operators/ntmc/
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Districts
      - definition:
        - link "Tucheng":
          - /url: /rail/stations/bl03/
        - text: ", Sanxia, Yingge"
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Opened
      - definition:
        - text: 30 June 2026
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Free trial until
      - definition:
        - text: 31 August 2026
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Stations
      - definition:
        - text: "12"
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Structure
      - definition:
        - text: Fully elevated
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
      - term: Automation
      - definition:
        - text: Driverless
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Interchanges
      - definition:
        - text: Dingpu (
        - link "Bannan Line":
          - /url: /rail/lines/bannan-line/
        - text: ), Yingge (TRA)
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Taiwan opened a new railway five weeks ago and, as of this page's writing, you can still ride it for nothing: tap in with any stored-value card and the fare is zero until the end of August"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . The Sanying Line is New Taipei's own metro — built by the city, run by its own metro company — and it gives Sanxia and Yingge, two districts that have watched the MRT map grow around them for thirty years, stations of their own.
    - heading "What opened, exactly" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The line runs 14.29 km on a fully elevated alignment through
      - link "Tucheng":
        - /url: /rail/stations/bl03/
      - text: ", Sanxia and Yingge, with 12 stations"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: . Trains are driverless, two-car sets
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: ", running about every 6 minutes at peak and 8 off-peak, and the end-to-end run takes roughly half an hour"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "It connects to the rest of the network at both ends of its purpose: at"
      - link "Dingpu":
        - /url: /rail/stations/bl01/
      - text: ", riders change to the"
      - link "Bannan Line":
        - /url: /rail/lines/bannan-line/
      - text: and the Taipei core; at Yingge, to the TRA main line
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . That pair of transfers is the line's argument — the districts it serves previously reached the MRT by bus or car, and the city's stated case for the line is the commuting time it removes.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Service opened on 30 June 2026, with the first train in the early afternoon and a
      - strong: free trial period to 31 August
      - text: ": any electronic stored-value card tapped in and out rides free"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . Trial hours began at 10:00–20:00 and were extended from the start of August to 08:00–22:00
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: — worth knowing, because most guidance still quotes the original shorter day. When charging begins, fares run NT$20 to NT$35 by distance
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - heading "The first month" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The operator's engineering bureau put the first month's ridership at over
      - strong: 750,000 journeys
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: — for a two-car driverless line serving two outer districts, on restricted hours, a figure that surprised the line's own planners into saying so publicly.
    - paragraph:
      - text: On 25 July the city unveiled an
      - strong: indigenous-themed painted train
      - text: ": Amis clothing patterns on the exterior, an interior built around Amis weaving culture, and character figures from the Atayal and Paiwan peoples"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: . No published schedule says when it runs, which is presumably part of why chasing it has become a small local sport — but that last observation is this page editorialising, not a sourced claim.
    - heading "What is not yet on this page" [level=2]
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - strong: Rolling stock detail.
        - text: The trains are reported as Hitachi-built, but the accounts found so far disagree on which Hitachi plant built them, and the fleet size and speed figures circulating are single-source. A dedicated rolling stock page waits until the operator's or builder's own record can be cited. Marked TBC above rather than borrowed.
      - listitem:
        - strong: The depot.
        - text: zh.wikipedia names 三峽機廠 in Sanxia
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
        - text: ; nothing else about it is established here yet.
      - listitem:
        - strong: Station data.
        - text: This site's station registry, maps and geometry come from the government TDX platform, and the Sanying Line's stations are not yet in the extract this site builds from. Integrating them — codes, coordinates, interchanges, a strip map for this page — is the next data task, and until then this page deliberately has no station list rather than a hand-typed one.
      - listitem:
        - strong: The extension.
        - text: An extension toward Bade in Taoyuan has Executive Yuan approval
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
        - text: ; its state of construction is not established here.
    - heading "Why this page exists already" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "This site's usual pattern is depth before breadth — one line finished properly before the next is started. The Sanying Line jumps the queue for a reason: it is five weeks old, English coverage is effectively nonexistent, and the facts above are the ones that rot fastest — trial dates, hours, fares. They are cited to the operator's own announcement, snapshotted, and dated, so that when the trial ends this page can say what changed rather than quietly rewriting itself."

- main:
  - article:

      - text: ·

      - text: The Matra dispute
    - heading "The Matra dispute" [level=1]
    - paragraph: Two disputes thirteen years apart, usually told as one — the test-track fires an engineering change explains, the seventeen-year lawsuit Matra won, and the walkout that taught Taipei how to buy its next railway.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taiwan's first metro line was bought as a French turnkey system in 1988, caught fire twice on the test track in 1993, opened in 1996 more than four years late, and lost its builder's maintenance staff not long afterwards
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: . Seventeen years after the signing, the Supreme Court ordered Taipei to pay Matra roughly
      - strong: NT$1.64 billion
      - text: ", and the city paid"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - paragraph: Almost all tellings run this together into one story about a French company storming off. It is two stories, thirteen years apart, and telling them apart is the point of this page.
    - region "Quick facts":
      - link "BR":
        - /url: /rail/lines/wenhu-line/
      - link "Wenhu Line":
        - /url: /rail/lines/wenhu-line/
      - text: 文湖線
      - term: Client
      - definition:
        - text: DORTS, Taipei City Government
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Contractor
      - definition:
        - text: Matra Transport
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Contract signed

        - superscript:

            - /url: "#ref-6"
      - term: Contract value

        - superscript:

            - /url: "#ref-6"
      - term: Line opened
      - definition:
        - text: 28 March 1996
        - superscript:
          - link "[9]":
            - /url: "#ref-9"
      - term: Arbitration award
      - definition:
        - text: 6 October 1993
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":

      - term: Final judgment

        - superscript:

        - superscript:

            - /url: "#ref-1"
    - heading "Two disputes, not one" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - strong: The delay claim, 1988–2005.
      - text: Matra sued for the cost of a contract that ran years longer than it was written for, because the civil works its equipment depended on were late — the claim arises, in 自由時報's words, 「因土木工程部分包商施工延誤，連帶造成馬特拉的工期延長，增加成本費用」
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . This is the dispute that went to arbitration in 1993 and was still before the Supreme Court in 2005
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . It is about money and contract law, and
      - strong: Matra won it
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - strong: The withdrawal, 1996–97.
      - text: After the line opened, Matra pulled its technical staff out of Taiwan and stopped maintaining the system
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: . This is the dispute everybody remembers — the one that produced the most famous sentence said about the
      - link "Taipei Metro":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
      - text: ", and the one that steered the procurement that followed."
    - paragraph:
      - text: "They are connected: the withdrawal happened because the delay claim had poisoned the relationship. But they are not the same event, and the NT$1.64 billion that circulates belongs to the first, not the second"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - heading "The contract" [level=2]
    - table:
      - rowgroup:
        - row "Term Agreed Source":
          - columnheader "Term"
          - columnheader "Agreed"
          - columnheader "Source"
      - rowgroup:
        - row "Matra selected as preferred bidder 20 April 1988 [6]":
          - cell "Matra selected as preferred bidder"
          - cell "20 April 1988"
          - cell "[6]":
            - superscript:
              - link "[6]":
                - /url: "#ref-6"
        - row "Negotiations concluded 25 June 1988 [6]":
          - cell "Negotiations concluded"
          - cell "25 June 1988"
          - cell "[6]":
            - superscript:
              - link "[6]":
                - /url: "#ref-6"
        - row "Contract signed 13 July 1988 [6][1]":
          - cell "Contract signed"
          - cell "13 July 1988"
          - cell "[6][1]":
            - superscript:
              - link "[6]":
                - /url: "#ref-6"
            - superscript:
              - link "[1]":
                - /url: "#ref-1"
        - row "Value ≈ NT$7.87 billion [6]":
          - cell "Value"
          - cell "≈ NT$7.87 billion"
          - cell "[6]":
            - superscript:
              - link "[6]":
                - /url: "#ref-6"
        - row "Scope Muzha Line E&M, design, 51 two-car sets, testing, training [6]":
          - cell "Scope"
          - cell "Muzha Line E&M, design, 51 two-car sets, testing, training"
          - cell "[6]":
            - superscript:
              - link "[6]":
                - /url: "#ref-6"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The scope matters more than the number. Taipei did not hire a contractor to electrify a railway; it bought a complete driverless system — vehicles, control, design and testing in one contract
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: ". That single fact decides both halves of this story: it is why the courts eventually read the deal the way they did, and it is why losing the vendor meant losing the means to run the railway."
    - paragraph:
      - text: 黃令名's account of the tender is that it was deliberately written to a 「歐美標準」 — a European-or-American standard rather than a US-only one — which opened it to European bidders, and that VAL was then the most mature automated system on the market
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: . He also records, without endorsing, that the award fed rumours connecting it to arms purchases from France
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: . He reports them as rumours; so does this page.
    - heading "The fires, and the engineering behind them" [level=2]
    - heading "Two fires, and what the builder calls them" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - strong: There were two, four and a half months apart
      - text: ", and the second is recorded as exactly that: 「1993年5月5日：辛亥站前發生火燒車事件」 and 「1993年9月24日：發生"
      - strong: 第二次
      - text: 火燒車事件」
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: . A second vehicle-fire incident. 自由時報 in 2005 said the same from the other end, describing 「接連被兩把大火燒得焦黑的電聯車」 — trains burned black by two successive fires
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: That matters more than the count suggests.
      - strong: One fire during testing is an accident. Two is a pattern
      - text: ", and a pattern is what makes the rest of the year explicable: MOTC halting all work, the Control Yuan impeaching eight officials the following February, and a city council that then spent eight years refusing to let the same technology go north."
    - paragraph:
      - strong: DORTS's own project record does not use the word fire at all.
      - text: It says 「木柵線於82年系統測試階段發生
      - strong: 輪胎起火意外事故
      - text: 」 — during the Muzha Line's system-testing phase in 1993, a
      - strong: tyre ignition accident
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: ". One noun phrase, no date, no count, and it is the most precise wording anyone has used about the mechanism: what burned was a tyre, not a train."
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Which of the two it refers to, the builder does not say.
      - text: It may be either, or it may be the class of event rather than an instance of it. This page does not choose, because there is nothing to choose from.
    - paragraph: So the two vocabularies are kept side by side rather than collapsed. The gap between 輪胎起火 and 火燒車 is roughly the gap between "an overheated tyre ignited" and "the train was on fire", which from a platform look identical — and the more precise phrasing belongs to the organisation that was impeached over it, which is worth seeing at the same time as the other.
    - heading "The mechanism" [level=3]
    - paragraph: There is an actual mechanism here, and it is better than "the French trains kept catching fire".
    - paragraph:
      - text: The trains were designed and run in France as
      - strong: two-car units
      - text: . For Taipei the capacity specification became
      - strong: four cars
      - text: ", and the automatic train control was not redesigned to match — two two-car units were coupled and run on a shared signal path"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: ". When the link between them failed, the units disagreed about what to do next: in 黃令名's reconstruction the lead unit began to move while the trailing unit, having heard nothing, kept its brakes locked"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: ; in 自由時報's, braking seized one axle pair while another drove on — 「煞車咬死，輪胎空轉摩擦過熱起火燃燒」
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The two accounts differ in that detail and agree in everything that matters: a capacity change outran the signalling design, brakes dragged, and on rubber tyres against a concrete running surface, dragging makes heat and heat makes fire"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: . On a steel-wheel railway the same failure produces wheel flats and noise. The fires were the tyres' version.
    - paragraph: Two independent tellings, three years apart, is decent corroboration for a causal chain — but neither is an accident investigation, and none has been found. That gap is flagged again at the foot of this page.
    - heading "The recorded incidents" [level=3]
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - text: 5 May 1993
        - strong: First fire
        - text: ", during testing, 辛亥站前 — in front of"
        - link "BR05":
          - /url: /rail/stations/br05/
        - text: Xinhai
        - superscript:
          - link "[5]":
            - /url: "#ref-5"
        - text: ; attributed to 「煞車系統故障及人為疏忽」 — brake failure and human error; Matra apologised publicly on 14 May
        - superscript:
          - link "[6]":
            - /url: "#ref-6"
      - listitem:
        - text: From April 1993 Cracked cap beams found at
        - link "BR07":
          - /url: /rail/stations/br07/
        - text: Liuzhangli,
        - link "BR03":
          - /url: /rail/stations/br03/
        - text: Wanfang Community and elsewhere; investigation and reinforcement demanded.
        - superscript:
          - link "[6]":
            - /url: "#ref-6"
      - listitem:
        - text: 19 June 1993 Testing suspended after further smoke and fire events; in July Matra attributed them to 「晶片問題」 — chip faults.
        - superscript:
          - link "[6]":
            - /url: "#ref-6"
      - listitem:
        - text: 24 September 1993
        - strong: Second fire
        - text: ", recorded as 第二次火燒車事件, between"
        - link "BR07":
          - /url: /rail/stations/br07/
        - text: Liuzhangli and
        - link "BR06":
          - /url: /rail/stations/br06/
        - text: Linguang.
        - superscript:
          - link "[5]":
            - /url: "#ref-5"
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":
            - /url: "#ref-2"
      - listitem:
        - text: 1 July 1994 Matra stops work, resuming on 23 July.
        - superscript:
          - link "[6]":
            - /url: "#ref-6"
      - listitem:
        - text: 25 August 1994 Final inspections conclude.
        - superscript:
          - link "[6]":
            - /url: "#ref-6"
      - listitem:
        - text: 28 March 1996 The line opens — four and a quarter years after the completion date the contract envisaged.
        - superscript:
          - link "[9]":
            - /url: "#ref-9"
        - superscript:
          - link "[6]":
            - /url: "#ref-6"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Most of this chronology is one encyclopedia entry deep
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: ". The two fires themselves are better anchored: 自由時報 places them in May and September of 1993"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: ", and its 2005 commentary invokes 「接連被兩把大火 燒得焦黑的電聯車，以及將近兩百根暴露著裂縫的捷運支柱」 — two burned trains and nearly two hundred cracked columns"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: Those cracked columns deserve their own sentence. Cap beams are civil works, not Matra's electrical and mechanical scope — they belong to the other contractors on the project
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . The same programme that burned Matra's trains in public was also, more quietly, running late underneath them, and that lateness is what Matra's claim was made of.
    - heading "The arbitration, and seventeen years of litigation" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: From the 自由時報 report of the final judgment
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: "— the best-documented part of the whole affair and the part least often told accurately:"
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - text: Matra's claim 「廿多億元」 — over NT$2 billion, for time added by others' delays
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - listitem:
        - text: Negotiation Collapsed
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - listitem:
        - text: "Arbitration, 6 October 1993 For Matra: awards in NT dollars, US dollars and francs totalling ≈"
        - strong: NT$1.025 billion
        - text: ", plus 5% annual interest"
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - listitem:
        - text: DORTS sues to annul the award Loses; the Supreme Court upholds the award in November 2000
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - listitem:
        - text: "DORTS resists enforcement Argues the claim is time-barred: a works contract carries a short limitation period, expired since 1998."
        - strong: Two courts agree.
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - listitem:
        - text: Supreme Court remands The High Court, rehearing the case, reclassifies the contract as 「買賣、承攬的混合契約」 — a mixed sale-and-works contract — carrying a
        - strong: fifteen-year
        - text: limitation. Matra is in time.
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - listitem:
        - text: Supreme Court, 22 July 2005 DORTS's appeal dismissed. Principal plus twelve years' interest ≈
        - strong: NT$1.64 billion.
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Sit with the pivot for a moment, because it is the best irony in Taipei's transit history. The city very nearly won: two courts accepted that Matra had simply waited too long. What defeated it was the"
      - emphasis: character of the contract
      - text: — the rehearing found that a deal covering route definition, structural design, and the purchase, installation and testing of vehicles and equipment was not mere contracting but a purchase of a system, with a purchase's fifteen-year limitation
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
      - strong: "Taipei lost the lawsuit for the same reason it had lost control of its railway: it had bought a turnkey system."
      - text: The clause that cost it NT$1.64 billion
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: and the lock-in that cost it its maintainer were the same decision, read twice.
    - paragraph:
      - emphasis: The judgment itself has not been read here — only the reporting of it. The full sequence between 2000 and 2005 involves stages this page has deliberately left undated, because the accounts found disagree on the intermediate chronology and the judgment text would settle it. See the foot of the page.
    - heading "The withdrawal, and the year nobody can pin down" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - strong: That Matra pulled its people out is not in dispute. When, exactly, is.
    - paragraph:
      - text: 〈木柵線〉 says it happened 「在通車兩個月之後」 — two months after the March 1996 opening, so around May 1996
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: . The same encyclopedia's article on the through line says it happened in
      - strong: "1997"
      - text: ", after a contract dispute, when Matra 「將技術人員全數撤離，不再提供維修服務」"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: . Both readings circulate; this site could not separate them, and no contemporaneous news report of the walkout itself has been found. One reconciliation — staff leaving through 1996, maintenance formally ending in 1997 — is plausible and is exactly the kind of guess this site does not publish as fact.
      - strong: No year is asserted here.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "What the period looked like from inside city hall has, since March 2026, an account from the mayor himself: 陳水扁 describes a fight over spare-parts pricing — Matra quoting NT$10,000 for a patented rubbish bin is his example — and the company using the threat of pulling its technicians as leverage in the renegotiation"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: . A memoir published on the line's thirtieth anniversary is a primary source with an interest in its own story, and it is cited here as that; but note that it frames the withdrawal not as a sudden exit but as a
      - strong: negotiating instrument that was eventually used
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: 商業周刊 was writing about the relationship under the title 「恩怨情仇」 — grudges and feuds — by 30 May 1996, six weeks after opening
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: ". That article is the closest thing to a contemporaneous account of the collapse; it is paywalled, has not been read past its opening here, and is cited only for what its date and title establish: whatever the formal end date, the marriage was publicly over within weeks of the trains carrying passengers"
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: .
    - heading "Keeping a metro nobody would maintain" [level=2]
    - paragraph: What Taipei was left holding was a driverless system whose builder would not service it — proprietary control software, proprietary parts, and no second source for either.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "黃令名's account — and this is his research speaking, singular and attributed, not a settled record — is that Taiwanese engineers kept the line running by 「偷偷複製法方半成品的列車控制程式、請台廠製造甚至赴光華商場取得 電子零件」: covertly copying the French side's half-finished train control software, commissioning parts from Taiwanese manufacturers, and sourcing electronics at Guanghua Market, Taipei's consumer electronics bazaar"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: . He calls this 「技術能動性」 — technological agency — and it is fair to say his article exists to make that argument
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "陳水扁's retelling corroborates the substance from the client's side, minus the market stalls: replacement components were developed with 中研院, 中科院, 工研院 and private industry until every part had a domestic alternative, cheaper than the originals"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: . Between a scholar's account of improvisation and a politician's account of mobilisation sits what actually happened; both agree the parts stopped coming from France and the trains kept running.
    - paragraph:
      - text: For the cost of the other road, 黃令名 points at Jacksonville, Florida — a city that faced a comparable dead end with its own Matra system and resolved it by demolition, rebuilding with a Bombardier monorail
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: . Taipei's choice to keep the French railway alive without the French is the road that led, eventually, to this site's
      - link "Wenhu Line":
        - /url: /rail/lines/wenhu-line/
      - text: page describing one seamless operation.
    - heading "The political ledger" [level=2]
    - blockquote:
      - paragraph:
        - text: 「馬特拉不拉，我們自己拉」
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":
            - /url: "#ref-2"
        - superscript:
          - link "[4]":
            - /url: "#ref-4"
      - paragraph:
        - text: 陳水扁, then Mayor of Taipei —
        - emphasis: if Matra won't pull, we'll pull it ourselves
    - paragraph: The dispute consumed three mayors, one per act.
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - strong: 黃大洲
        - text: presided over the fires. 自由時報's commentary holds that the 木柵線 debacle 「間接導致了當時台北市長黃大洲的敗選下台」 — indirectly cost him the 1994 election
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: . A newspaper asserting why an election was lost is a genre with a poor record; the timing fits, the claim is widely repeated, and it is published here as the paper's judgment rather than a fact.
      - listitem:
        - strong: 陳水扁
        - text: opened the line on 28 March 1996
        - superscript:
          - link "[6]":
            - /url: "#ref-6"
        - text: and gave the affair the epitaph above. 自由時報 canonises it as his 名言
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":
            - /url: "#ref-2"
        - text: ; his own account of saying it, thirty years later, has it blurted out mid-crisis in the parts-pricing fight
        - superscript:
          - link "[4]":
            - /url: "#ref-4"
        - text: . The line is quoted everywhere and dated almost nowhere — no contemporaneous record of the moment of utterance has been found, and its setting rests on the speaker's memory.
      - listitem:
        - strong: 馬英九
        - text: was mayor when the final bill arrived in July 2005, and said the city would pay what the judgment required
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: . The DORTS director, 常岐德, declined all interviews and switched off his phone
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: ". The commentary's arithmetic was blunter: 「全民買單繳『學費』，足足要花十六億 四千萬元」 — the public pays the tuition, all NT$1.64 billion of it"
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: .
    - 'heading "What it changed: buying the Neihu extension" [level=2]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: When the line's northern half came to be tendered, DORTS changed the two things that had produced the trap, on 黃令名's analysis of the procurement
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: ":"
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - strong: CBTC was specified
        - text: — communications-based train control, an open signalling approach — rather than an extension of Matra's proprietary fixed-block system
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
        - text: .
      - listitem:
        - strong: Civil works and E&M were let together
        - text: ", as one integrated contract, rather than split across contractors whose mutual delays had just spent seventeen years in court"
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
        - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: By then the incumbent was not even Matra. Siemens had taken control of Matra Transport International in the 1990s — 95% by October 1998
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: — and completed the takeover in November 2001, renaming the business Siemens Transportation Systems
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: . VAL was now a Siemens product, and a tender written around VAL would have had exactly one credible bidder. 黃令名's argument is that the CBTC-plus-turnkey structure existed precisely so that Siemens could not name its price as the only party able to extend the existing system
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: . Procurement rationales are the kind of thing institutions tidy up afterwards, and his is the only account found
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: — but it is consistent with what was actually bought.
    - paragraph:
      - text: What was bought was Bombardier. And here the engineering gets genuinely elegant, because Bombardier could not supply a VAL — VAL belonged to a competitor. So it built the
      - link "Innovia APM 256":
        - /url: /rail/rolling-stock/innovia-apm-256-c370/
      - text: ": a people mover dimensioned to a French railway it had no rights to, matching the running-surface spacing, the side guide bars and the 750 V supply taken off them, with a car body 20 mm narrower than the"
      - link "VAL256":
        - /url: /rail/rolling-stock/val256/
      - text: it would run beside
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: . The incumbent's guideway became the tender's interface specification.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The last act was the cutover. Rather than run two signalling systems, the whole line switched to Bombardier's CITYFLO 650 on the day the extension opened —
      - strong: 4 July 2009
      - text: — and the 1996 Matra fleet was withdrawn that same day for conversion, returning on 26 December 2010 after eighteen months with its French control system replaced
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: . 黃令名 adds — his account alone; nothing else found says it — that CITYFLO had been tested at night on the Muzha Line's own tracks while the Matra system carried passengers by day
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: . It is a striking detail, it is single-source, and those two properties are related; it is recorded here with its attribution showing.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The last Matra-controlled train ran thirteen years after Matra stopped maintaining any of them. Nobody from the company was there to see it, and by then there was no company: the name had been gone from the rail business for eight years"
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: .
    - separator
    - heading "What is not established" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "The gaps, recorded so they are searched for rather than papered over:"
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - strong: The contract itself.
        - text: No tender documents, competing bids or evaluation records were found; they would sit in DORTS's construction archive.
      - listitem:
        - strong: The judgments.
        - text: Taiwan's court decisions are indexed and searchable, and the 22 July 2005 Supreme Court civil judgment ought to be retrievable; it would move the whole litigation section from reportage to primary record, and settle the intermediate dates this page declines to give. The single highest-value follow-up here.
      - listitem:
        - strong: A contemporaneous report of the withdrawal
        - text: ", which would close the question above of which year it happened in"
        - superscript:
          - link "[6]":
            - /url: "#ref-6"
        - superscript:
          - link "[7]":
            - /url: "#ref-7"
        - text: .
      - listitem:
        - strong: Any accident investigation
        - text: into the 1993 fires, which would confirm or kill the coupling explanation two secondary sources agree on. DORTS's own classification of the testing-phase incident — 輪胎起火意外事故, a tyre ignition accident
        - superscript:
          - link "[9]":
            - /url: "#ref-9"
        - text: — is as close as the primary record gets, and it names no date, no unit and no location.
      - listitem:
        - strong: Which fire DORTS's 輪胎起火意外事故 describes.
        - text: The builder names an incident and gives it no date and no ordinal
        - superscript:
          - link "[9]":
            - /url: "#ref-9"
        - text: . There were two. Nothing found says which, or whether the phrase names the class rather than an instance.
      - listitem:
        - strong: Matra's side.
        - text: Every substantive source on this page is Taiwanese. The French trade press of the day, Lagardère's archive and Siemens's own history of the VAL business would give the other account, and none has been found. Its absence is the largest structural bias in this page, and it is not a small one.

    - paragraph: Eleven stations, running the same way as the operating codes, in a series of their own. That is what a separate design and contract package looks like from the outside.
    - heading "The station that does not fit" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Look at the boundary. The Neihu section is BR13 to BR24 — twelve stations. The B series has eleven.
      - strong: BR13 Songshan Airport is a Neihu-section station carrying a Muzha-section number
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The chronology says why it might be. Songshan Airport was not in the original scheme: MOTC directed a study on serving the airport directly in February 2000, the Executive Yuan agreed in principle on 1 August 2001, and the funding was approved on 4 January 2002"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . By then the Neihu section's B series had been allocated to the stations that already existed on paper.
    - paragraph: A station added to a project after its numbers were handed out has to go somewhere. This one went into the other series, at its head.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: That last step is this site reading the table, not DORTS explaining it.
      - text: The addition date is the builder's; the inference about the numbering is ours, and it is offered as a reading rather than a fact. What the table shows without interpretation is that the number is in the wrong series for the section the station is in.
    - heading "Why any of it matters" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taipei's network was not designed and then built. It was built project by project, each with its own budget, contractor, systems supplier and drawing set, and then operated as one railway afterwards. Almost every oddity on this site traces back to that — two incompatible fleets on one line, a depot in the wrong district for its name, station numbers that jump 29 places on the
      - link "Zhonghe–Xinlu Line":
        - /url: /rail/lines/zhonghe-xinlu-line/
      - text: .
    - paragraph: The numbering is the cleanest evidence of it, because it is the seam left visible in the paperwork. The signs were made to be read by passengers on a finished railway. The drawings were made by two teams, working outward from their own starting points, years apart.
    - heading "Sources" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Every number on this page is transcribed from DORTS's own station table for the 文山內湖線 project
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . The station registry carries the engineering number as a field, so the diagram, the tables and the station pages read the same values and cannot drift apart.
    - region "References":
      - heading "References" [level=2]
      - paragraph: 1 of 2 sources on this page is primary — published by the operator, the builder or government.
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - link "Wenshan—Neihu Line":
            - /url: https://www.dorts.gov.taipei/cp.aspx?n=DBAC040496EFAB94
          - text: 文山內湖線 primary Taipei City Government, Department of Rapid Transit Systems (DORTS) accessed 2026-08-07
          - link "archived":
            - /url: https://web.archive.org/web/20260209210832/https://www.dorts.gov.taipei/cp.aspx?n=DBAC040496EFAB94
          - text: "The builder's own station table, which is where the engineering numbers come from: it lists 工程編號 against 車站編號 for all twenty-four stations, together with addresses and exit counts. Every number on this page is transcribed from it. The same page also carries the Songshan Airport station's chronology — MOTC directs a study in February 2000, the Executive Yuan agrees in principle on 1 August 2001, the Public Construction Commission approves the funding on 4 January 2002."
        - listitem:
          - link "Wenhu line":
            - /url: https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-tw/文湖線
          - text: 文湖線 secondary 維基百科 (Chinese Wikipedia) accessed 2026-08-07
          - link "archived":
            - /url: https://web.archive.org/web/20250714045049/https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-tw/文湖線
          - text: Cited here only for the two dates the operating code arrived on — the line number and colour on 11 October 2014, the two-letter station code in October 2016. Neither is in DORTS's project record, which stops at the opening; a TRTC announcement would be the primary source and has not been found.

    - region "Quick facts":
      - link "BR":

        - /url: /rail/lines/wenhu-line/
      - text: 文湖線

        - text: Matra Transport, with GEC Alsthom
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Family
      - definition: VAL
      - term: Operator

      - term: Built
      - definition:
        - text: 1990—1993
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: In service
      - definition:
        - text: 28 March 1996 —
        - superscript:
          - link "[6]":
            - /url: "#ref-6"
      - term: Depot
      - definition:
        - link "Muzha":
          - /url: /rail/depots/muzha-depot/
        - text: and
        - link "Neihu":
          - /url: /rail/depots/neihu-depot/
        - superscript:
          - link "[7]":
            - /url: "#ref-7"
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Stub page.
      - text: This entry is an outline. Figures marked
      - emphasis: TBC
      - text: still need to be checked against a primary source before publication.
    - region "Formation":
      - heading "Formation" [level=2]
      - 'img "Formation: Mc1=M2 + M2=Mc1"': Mc1 M2 M2 Mc1
      - paragraph: 4 cars · 2 units of 2 · one unit coupling cab
    - paragraph: A train delivered in the early 1990s is still running the line, and almost nothing tells it what to do any more.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The VAL256 sets were built by Matra with GEC Alsthom between 1990 and 1993
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: and entered service with the Muzha Line on 28 March 1996
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: . The
      - code: "256"
      - text: is the car width in centimetres — 2,560 mm — and it is the wider of the two standard VAL profiles, the other being the 2,060 mm VAL206 used at Lille
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: .
    - heading "The re-signalling" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The conversion did not precede the
      - link "Neihu":
        - /url: /rail/stations/br19/
      - text: "extension — it was triggered by it, and the sequence is the story:"
    - table:
      - rowgroup:
        - row "Date Event":
          - columnheader "Date"
          - columnheader "Event"
      - rowgroup:
        - row "4 July 2009 The Neihu extension opens. The line switches to CITYFLO 650, the Matra system is cut off after thirteen years, and the VAL256 fleet comes out of service that day to begin conversion[1][5]":
          - cell "4 July 2009"
          - cell "The Neihu extension opens. The line switches to CITYFLO 650, the Matra system is cut off after thirteen years, and the VAL256 fleet comes out of service that day to begin conversion[1][5]":
            - text: The Neihu extension opens. The line switches to CITYFLO 650, the Matra system is cut off after thirteen years, and the VAL256 fleet
            - strong: comes out of service that day
            - text: to begin conversion
            - superscript:
              - link "[1]":
                - /url: "#ref-1"
            - superscript:
              - link "[5]":
                - /url: "#ref-5"
        - row "26 December 2010 Converted VAL256 units return to passenger service, running alongside the Innovia fleet[1]":
          - cell "26 December 2010"
          - cell "Converted VAL256 units return to passenger service, running alongside the Innovia fleet[1]":
            - text: Converted VAL256 units return to passenger service, running alongside the Innovia fleet
            - superscript:
              - link "[1]":
                - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: So for nearly eighteen months the whole 24-station line ran on the Bombardier fleet alone, while the trains that had opened the railway sat in a depot having their control system replaced. Why the line was re-signalled at all — and why by a competitor of the system's owner — is told on
      - link "The Matra dispute":
        - /url: /rail/history/matra-dispute/
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The original equipment was a fixed-block ATC/ATO system derived from the MAGGALY technology on Lyon Metro line D
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: ; what replaced it is a moving-block communications-based system.
    - heading "Design" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: VAL vehicles run on rubber tyres over concrete running surfaces, and are guided from the
      - strong: sides
      - text: ", not the centre: pairs of horizontal wheels bear outward against lateral guide bars — H-section steel, set roughly 200 mm above the running surface on either side of the vehicle — and those same bars carry the 750 V supply, which is why a VAL guideway needs no separate conductor rail"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: VAL's own successor went the other way. The NeoVal generation Siemens announced in 2006
      - emphasis: is
      - text: centrally guided, on a single rail similar to Translohr's
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: . Central guidance is VAL's future, not its past, and Taipei has the past.
    - heading "The formation is not fixed" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Cars are delivered and counted in pairs — DORTS bought 51 of them under contract CC350
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: — and two pairs make a four-car train. But
      - strong: the pairs are not permanently married into sets
      - text: ": zh.wikipedia describes this fleet as 「非固定編組」, a non-fixed formation, with a train made up of four consecutively-numbered cars rather than of one unchanging four-car unit"
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: That detail does more work than it looks.
      - link "TRTC":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
      - text: "'s own announcement of the seat-removal programme counts"
      - strong: 25 four-car trains
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: ", and 25 trains is 50 pairs against a fleet of 51. If the sets were fixed, that odd pair would be a permanent orphan needing an explanation. If the formation is not fixed, there is nothing to explain — the cars run as 25 trains"
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: and which cars those are is a maintenance question rather than a fact about the fleet
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Confidence is Medium and the page does not overstate it.
      - text: The pair counts and the train count are both primary; 非固定編組 is one encyclopedia, and no manufacturer or operator document found says it. It is also the reading that resolves the
      - link "line-level arithmetic problem":
        - /url: /rail/lines/wenhu-line/
      - text: without requiring a train formed from both fleets, which is a reason to want it to be true and therefore a reason to mark it carefully.
    - heading "Fleet history" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Ordered for the Muzha Line and in service from its opening on 28 March 1996, originally working BR01 through BR12 only. Since December 2010 the fleet has run the full route alongside the
      - link "Innovia APM 256 (C370)":
        - /url: /rail/rolling-stock/innovia-apm-256-c370/
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - emphasis: Delivery dates by unit, and the scope of the re-signalling work on each set, are still to be confirmed.
    - heading "Depot allocation" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Maintained at
      - link "Muzha Depot":
        - /url: /rail/depots/muzha-depot/
      - text: ", beside BR01 , which also stables Innovia sets"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: .
    - heading "Corrections" [level=2]
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - strong: This page previously said the fleet was re-signalled ahead of the 2009 extension.
        - text: "That inverts the sequence: the conversion began the day the extension opened and the fleet was out of service until December 2010"
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: .
      - listitem:
        - strong: This page previously said VAL vehicles are guided by horizontal wheels bearing on a central rail.
        - text: They are side-guided
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
        - superscript:
          - link "[4]":
            - /url: "#ref-4"
        - text: . The likely origin of the error is the NeoVal succession — the
        - emphasis: later
        - text: generation is centrally guided, and the two were run together here.

      - term: Grade
      - definition:
        - text: Third-level depot
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":
            - /url: "#ref-2"
      - term: Fleet based
      - definition:
        - link "VAL256":

        - text: and
        - link "Innovia APM 256":
          - /url: /rail/rolling-stock/innovia-apm-256-c370/
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":
            - /url: "#ref-2"
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Stub page.
      - text: This entry is an outline. Figures marked
      - emphasis: TBC
      - text: still need to be checked against a primary source before publication.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Every train on the Taipei network traces back to this site. When the
      - link "Muzha Line":
        - /url: /rail/lines/wenhu-line/
      - text: opened in 1996 there was nowhere else — no other depot, no other line, no other fleet. 木柵機廠 was the whole of the system's engineering capability, sitting at the foot of the hills beside BR01 .
    - paragraph:
      - text: Thirteen years later it stopped being that. When
      - link "Neihu Depot":
        - /url: /rail/depots/neihu-depot/
      - text: opened in 2009 it took over as the line's full-function depot and as its primary operations control centre
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: ", and"
      - link "Muzha":
        - /url: /rail/stations/br02/
      - text: was regraded from a fifth-level to a
      - strong: third-level
      - text: depot
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: . The oldest depot on the network is now the junior of the line's two
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: .
    - heading "Facilities" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS lists storage, maintenance, operations control, washing, lineside maintenance and parts warehousing
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . zh.wikipedia adds the buildings — a stabling yard, a workshop, a plant room, the control centre, a traction substation, a main substation, emergency power, a pumping station and a test track — with
      - strong: 12 stabling roads holding 84 pairs
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: .
    - paragraph: Eighty-four pairs is a striking number against a line whose entire fleet is 152 pairs, and it rests on one source. It should be checked before anything is built on it.
    - paragraph:
      - emphasis:
        - text: "Not established: what heavy overhaul is done here rather than at"
        - link "Neihu":
          - /url: /rail/stations/br19/
        - text: ", and whether either depot does it at all rather than contracting it out."
    - heading "Allocation" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The best available source says Muzha stables
      - strong: both
      - text: fleets —
      - link "VAL256":
        - /url: /rail/rolling-stock/val256/
      - text: and
      - link "Innovia APM 256":
        - /url: /rail/rolling-stock/innovia-apm-256-c370/
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: — so the line's allocation is not a clean one-fleet-per-depot split.
      - link "Neihu Depot":
        - /url: /rail/depots/neihu-depot/
      - text: is the Innovia fleet's principal base.
    - heading "Access" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Not open to the public.
      - emphasis: Any public viewing points or open-day arrangements to be added.
    - heading "Corrections" [level=2]
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - strong: This page previously said Muzha was home to the VAL256 fleet alone.
        - text: That one-fleet-per-depot split was never sourced; it was tidy, and wrong. The best available source says the depot stables both types
        - superscript:

        - text: ", and the Allocation section now matches the source rather than the assumption."

  - heading "The network" [level=1]
  - paragraph: 10 lines, 180 stations. 9 of the lines are drawn below from Taiwan MOTC route geometry; the Sanying Line is newer than MOTC’s extract, so its 12 stations are outside that station count and it is not on the map. Colours are the official ones each operator publishes — not the values circulating in English-language sources, which are all slightly wrong.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: The Sanying Line is not drawn.
    - text: It opened on 30 June 2026. The New Taipei Metro line records this map is built from carry a source update stamp of 23 May 2023 — nearly three years earlier — and return one line, the Circular Line. Rather than draw an alignment from a dataset that predates the railway, it is absent here and written up from the operator’s own announcement on its
    - link "line page":
      - /url: /rail/lines/sanying-line/
    - text: . It
    - emphasis: is
    - text: in the table below, in its own colour, taken from the operator’s LB line mark.
  - figure:
    - img
    - text: "Every line as surveyed, each labelled with its code at both ends — colour alone does not identify a line. Bannan blue and Airport MRT purple are indistinguishable to a reader with protanopia, and Tamsui red against Danhai red is the closest pair on the network even in normal colour vision, which is why every line carries its code. Interchange stations are ringed in black; termini are the outer dots. Branch track is drawn as a pale core of its parent's colour inside a hairline of the same colour darkened — a branch belongs to its line rather than being a line of its own, and the hairline is what gives the pale core a defined edge on the paper. 4 lines have one: Tamsui-Xinyi, Songshan-Xindian, Zhonghe-Xinlu and Danhai LRT. Where a line appears broken, the alignment across the gap is missing from the published geometry — those breaks are holes in the source data, not features of the network, and are left unbridged rather than joined with track we cannot evidence."
